messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 75
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: QA Engineer
- Trauma Type: Natural disaster
- Pcl5: 46

He is a 75-year-old Latin American man who has spent much of his life in the United States building a careful, orderly world for himself and his family. For many years he works as a QA engineer, a role that suits him well because he trusts checklists, repetition, and the quiet satisfaction of catching what others miss. He prides himself on being methodical at home too. His days have a rhythm: early coffee, a look over the news, a drive to work, and then the patient, exacting task of testing systems so that small failures do not become large ones.

That sense of order is shattered when the natural disaster comes through his community. The event itself happens fast, in a way that leaves little room for understanding while it is unfolding. One moment there is ordinary life; the next there is noise, fear, and the sense that the world has become unreliable. He does what he can to keep his wife safe, moving with urgency that later feels both instinctive and unreal to him. In the days that follow, he keeps replaying the scene in fragments: the sound, the shaking, the confusion of trying to decide what matters first. He remembers looking around and feeling that the familiar landscape no longer belongs to him.

Afterward, he tries to return to his routines, but the body does not cooperate with the mind’s wish for normalcy. He becomes tense when the weather changes, especially when he hears strong wind or sees warnings on the television. He finds himself scanning the sky and listening for sounds that other people seem to ignore. At night, he has trouble settling. He falls asleep only to wake abruptly, alert and disoriented, with his heart racing as if danger is still close. Sometimes he wakes from dreams that he cannot fully describe, only the feeling remains: dread, pressure in his chest, the sense that he is back in the middle of the disaster and cannot stop it.

He has always been the kind of man who likes problems to have clear solutions, and this makes his reactions especially frustrating to him. He notices that he is more irritable with his wife, though he quickly feels ashamed about it. He is quieter than before, less likely to sit and talk about what happened. When family members ask how he is doing, he often tells them he is fine, because he does not want to burden them and does not have words that seem adequate anyway. In private, he feels embarrassed by how often he startles at sudden noises. A slamming door, a sharp knock, even a dropped object can send a jolt through him. He tells himself he is being foolish, but his body responds before he can reason it away.

At work, he is still capable, but the effort costs him more. He double-checks his work more than he used to and has less patience when systems behave unpredictably. The logic of QA once brought him comfort; now unpredictability feels less like a technical issue and more like a threat. He worries about making mistakes, not because he has suddenly become careless, but because the disaster has shaken his confidence in his own steadiness. Some days he forces himself through the work with determination, and other days he catches himself staring at the screen, mind drifting back to that day when control seemed to vanish.

He and his wife have lived through many hardships together, and he draws strength from her presence, though he does not always know how to ask for comfort. He remains devoted to their shared routines, to meals at home, to the small acts of keeping life running. Even so, he is different now: more watchful, less rested, carrying a tension that sits under the surface of his days. The disaster has passed, but for him it continues to live on in the way he listens for danger, in the way he braces when the wind rises, and in the way ordinary life still feels, at times, as if it could break open again without warning.
